did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with the heading “For Solomon” and a request that the king receive justice and righteousness from the LORD, so that he may judge the people fairly.
Did you know? According to the psalm, the king’s role is not only to judge, but also to save the children of the poor and crush the oppressor.
Did you know? Just rule is portrayed through the image of rain: the king descends “like rain on mown grass” and like showers that water the earth.
Did you know? The flourishing of the righteous and the abundance of peace are presented in the psalm as blessings that continue throughout the king’s reign—“until there is no moon.”
Did you know? The boundaries of the king’s rule are described in expansive terms: “from sea to sea” and “from the river to the ends of the earth.”
Did you know? The psalm mentions kings from distant lands—Tarshish, the coastlands, Sheba, and Seba—who bring the king tribute and gifts.
Did you know? The central test of the king is how he treats the vulnerable: he rescues the poor who cry out for help and the needy who have no one to help them.
Did you know? The words “their blood is precious in his sight” emphasize that the lives of the poor and needy are valuable and worthy of protection in the king’s eyes.
Did you know? During the king’s reign, the psalm asks for agricultural abundance in the land: grain on the mountaintops and fruit that rustles like Lebanon, along with abundant growth in the cities.
Did you know? The final verse states explicitly, “The prayers of David son of Jesse are ended,” thereby concluding the collection of prayers attributed to David in this section.
